overview.title: Horizontal vs vertical partitioning; JAX for distributed training
overview.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world
overview.section: 18.2 Scaling up model training with multiple devices
overview.main_topic: Sharding a model: splitting by layers (horizontal) versus splitting each layer's tensors (vertical), illustrated by halving a Dense kernel across two GPUs
overview.central_idea: To fit a model across devices you shard it. Putting different layers on different devices (horizontal partitioning) forces activations to move between devices and can leave GPUs idle. Splitting every layer's kernel and bias across devices (vertical partitioning) uses the parallel structure of matmul and is almost always best for large models. In practice you combine this with data parallelism, and in Keras you do it on the JAX backend.
overview.importance: Vertical partitioning is the idea behind the LayoutMap sharding rules on p.577-578 ('shard the last dimension along the model axis'). This page shows by hand what Keras later automates.
learning_objectives: Contrast horizontal and vertical partitioning and explain the communication drawback of horizontal partitioning.
Derive the half-kernel and half-bias shapes when splitting Dense(64000) over two devices.
Explain why concatenating column-split matmul outputs reproduces the full layer output.
Explain how data and model parallelism are combined across 8 devices.
prerequisites: Matrix multiplication and the Dense layer as matmul(inputs, kernel) + bias (chapter 2)

summary:
The page finishes the parameter count for Listing 18.4: the last layer has about **512 million** parameters (the first about 1 billion). On **two small devices**, data parallelism is impossible because the model does not fit on either one. Instead you *split* one instance of the model across devices, which is called **sharding** or **partitioning**. There are two ways:

- **Horizontal partitioning**: each device runs *different layers*. GPU 0 runs the first `Dense`, GPU 1 the second. The drawback is **communication overhead**: the first layer's output must be copied to the second device before the second layer can run. If that output is large, this becomes a bottleneck and GPUs sit idle.
- **Vertical partitioning**: *each layer* is split across all devices. Layers are built from highly parallelizable `matmul` and `convolution` operations, so this is easy to implement and **almost always the best fit for large models**. For the first `Dense`, split the kernel along its last axis into two `(16000, 32000)` halves and the bias into two `(32000,)` halves. Each device computes `matmul(inputs, kernel) + bias` with its halves, and the two outputs are **concatenated**.

The code snippet slices `kernel` and `bias` and computes each half on `gpu:0` and `gpu:1` using `keras.device(...)` scopes. (The concatenation the text announces is not shown; see the review flag.)

In reality, data and model parallelism are **mixed**: the model is split across four devices and that split model is replicated twice, each copy handling a sub-batch, for **8 devices** (figure 18.2, p.575).

Section **18.2.2** then begins: the book covers only the **JAX backend**, which the authors call the most performant and scalable Keras backend 'by a mile' (the sentence continues on p.575).

concepts.name: Sharding (model partitioning)
concepts.definition: Splitting one model instance's variables and computation across multiple devices.
concepts.intuition: Cutting one large book into chapters held by different readers.
concepts.technical: Done per variable dimension: replicate or split along a mesh axis (p.577).
concepts.significance: The only way to train models larger than a device's memory.
concepts.example: The (16000, 64000) kernel cut into two (16000, 32000) shards.
concepts.misconception: That sharding means each device holds a different layer. That is only one form (horizontal); vertical sharding splits inside layers.

concepts.name: Horizontal partitioning
concepts.definition: Each device runs a different set of layers.
concepts.intuition: An assembly line: station 2 waits for station 1.
concepts.technical: Requires transferring activations between devices at stage boundaries; sequential dependence causes idle devices unless pipelined with micro-batches.
concepts.significance: Simple to reason about but often communication-bound.
concepts.example: GPU 0 runs Dense(64000), GPU 1 runs Dense(8000).
concepts.misconception: That it runs both devices at full speed. Without pipelining, only one stage works at a time.

concepts.name: Vertical partitioning
concepts.definition: Each layer's weight tensors are split across all devices; each device computes a slice of every layer.
concepts.intuition: Several painters each painting a different vertical strip of the same wall at the same time.
concepts.technical: Column-split matmul: x[W0|W1] = [xW0|xW1]; outputs concatenated along the feature axis.
concepts.significance: Almost always the best fit for large models, according to the book.
concepts.example: Half-kernels of shape (16000, 32000) on gpu:0 and gpu:1.
concepts.misconception: That it needs no communication. Inputs must be available on every device and outputs must be gathered (or kept sharded for the next layer).

concepts.name: Model parallelism
concepts.definition: Splitting a model across devices that process the same batch.
concepts.intuition: Share the model, not the data.
concepts.technical: Implemented by horizontal or vertical partitioning; combined with data parallelism in practice.
concepts.significance: Needed for models that do not fit on one device.
concepts.misconception: That it is used instead of data parallelism. Real setups use both.

math.title: Column-split matmul for vertical partitioning
math.source_text: split the kernel and bias of the first Dense layer into two halves so that each device only receives a kernel of shape (16000, 32000) (split along its last axis) and a bias of shape (32000,). You'd compute matmul(inputs, kernel) + bias with this half-kernel and half-bias for each device, and you'd merge the two outputs by concatenating them

variables.meaning: inputs, shape (batch, 16000), needed in full on both devices

math.operations: Each column of the output depends only on the matching column of W and entry of b, so the columns can be computed separately and placed side by side.
math.purpose: Shows why the per-device halves concatenated give exactly the full Dense output.
math.interpretation: Device k computes output units 32000k to 32000k + 31999 for all samples.
math.intuition: Each output neuron is an independent dot product; assign half the neurons to each GPU.
math.numerical_example: x = [1, 2], W = [[1, 0, 2, 1], [0, 1, 1, 3]], b = 0. Full xW = [1, 2, 4, 7]. Split W0 = first two columns gives [1, 2]; W1 = last two gives [4, 7]. Concatenated: [1, 2, 4, 7].

math.title: Shard shapes and per-device parameters
math.source_text: a kernel of shape (16000, 32000) (split along its last axis) and a bias of shape (32000,)
math.operations: Divide the last dimension by the number of devices.
math.purpose: Quantifies how much each device holds after vertical partitioning.
math.interpretation: Each GPU stores about 512 M parameters of the first layer (about 2 GB in float32) instead of about 1 B.
math.intuition: Halving the number of output units halves the layer's memory per device.

code.title: Splitting a Dense kernel and bias across two GPUs by hand
code.original_code:
half_kernel_0 = kernel[:, :32000]
half_bias_0 = bias[:32000]

half_kernel_1 = kernel[:, 32000:]
half_bias_1 = bias[32000:]

with keras.device("gpu:0"):
    half_output_0 = keras.ops.matmul(inputs, half_kernel_0) + half_bias_0

with keras.device("gpu:1"):
    half_output_1 = keras.ops.matmul(inputs, half_kernel_1) + half_bias_1
code.what_it_does: Slices the first Dense layer's kernel and bias into two column halves and computes each half of the layer output on a different GPU.

line_explanations.explanation: First half: all rows, columns 0-31,999 of the (16000, 64000) kernel, and bias entries 0-31,999.
Second half: columns 32,000-63,999 and the matching bias entries.
Inside a keras.device("gpu:0") scope, compute inputs @ half_kernel_0 + half_bias_0, a (batch, 32000) tensor.
The same on gpu:1 with the second halves. The two computations are independent and can run at the same time.

code.inputs_outputs: inputs (batch, 16000), kernel (16000, 64000), bias (64000,) -> half_output_0 and half_output_1, each (batch, 32000). Concatenating them along axis -1 gives (batch, 64000).
code.algorithm: Manual vertical (tensor) partitioning of one affine layer.
code.theory_link: Implements math m1. Keras automates exactly this with a LayoutMap entry such as (None, "model") for the kernel (p.577).

parameters.name: keras.device("gpu:k")
parameters.role: context manager placing the enclosed ops (and new tensors) on device k

pitfalls: The printed snippet stops before the merge. You still need keras.ops.concatenate([half_output_0, half_output_1], axis=-1).
Slicing a full kernel that already sits on one device defeats the purpose: in a real setup each half must be created on its own device from the start (which the LayoutMap API does).
The ReLU of the first layer is not applied here; it can be applied to each half independently.
inputs must be present on both devices, which costs a copy.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: complete the example with the merge step and a correctness check (small sizes)
import numpy as np
import keras
x = np.random.rand(4, 16).astype('float32')
kernel = np.random.rand(16, 64).astype('float32')
bias = np.random.rand(64).astype('float32')
h0 = keras.ops.matmul(x, kernel[:, :32]) + bias[:32]
h1 = keras.ops.matmul(x, kernel[:, 32:]) + bias[32:]
out = keras.ops.concatenate([h0, h1], axis=-1)
full = keras.ops.matmul(x, kernel) + bias
print(np.allclose(out, full, atol=1e-5))  # True

deeper.title: Horizontal vs vertical: who waits, what moves
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, for Listing 18.4 on two GPUs with batch 128:

**Horizontal.** (1) GPU 0 computes relu(x W1 + b1), a (128, 64000) tensor of about 33 MB in float32; GPU 1 is idle. (2) Copy the 33 MB to GPU 1. (3) GPU 1 computes the output layer; GPU 0 is idle. The backward pass repeats this in reverse with the activation gradient. Utilisation is at most about 50%.

**Vertical.** (1) Both GPUs hold x. (2) Each computes its (128, 32000) half of layer 1 at the same time. (3) For layer 2, each GPU holds half of the rows of W2, matching its half of the hidden units. Each computes a *partial* (128, 8000) product and the two partials are summed (all-reduce, about 4 MB). Both GPUs compute all the time, and the traffic is smaller.

This is why the book calls vertical partitioning 'almost always the best fit for large models'.

deeper.title: Why JAX for distribution
deeper.body: Beyond the book. JAX compiles the whole training step with XLA. With sharding annotations on arrays, XLA's SPMD partitioner rewrites the single-device program into a per-device program and inserts collectives (all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-reduce) where needed. This is why Keras can offer distribution through a few configuration objects (DataParallel, DeviceMesh, LayoutMap) without changing model or training code, as the book shows on p.575-578.

visualizations.title: Column split of a matmul, at toy size
visualizations.why: Each output column uses only one column of the kernel, which is why the half-kernels in the code produce independent halves of the output. Watch the columns of the product being computed separately.

misconceptions.claim: Putting each layer on its own GPU doubles speed with two GPUs.
misconceptions.correction: In horizontal partitioning the layers depend on each other in sequence, so devices take turns and activations must be copied; the book warns GPUs may sit idle.

misconceptions.claim: Vertical partitioning gives an approximation of the layer's output.
misconceptions.correction: Concatenating column-split matmul outputs is exactly equal to the full matmul (math m1).

misconceptions.claim: The printed snippet produces the full layer output.
misconceptions.correction: It produces two halves; the concatenation the text mentions must still be added.

Definitions of data and model parallelism.

later.note: Figure 18.2 (two replicas x four devices) and the DataParallel API.
LayoutMap: replicate or shard each variable dimension.
Rule of thumb: shard the last dimension along the model axis.

related_code.note: LayoutMap entries such as (None, "model") automate this split.

takeaways: Sharding/partitioning splits one model instance across devices when it does not fit on one.
Horizontal partitioning (layers per device) suffers from activation transfers and idle devices.
Vertical partitioning (split every layer's kernel) uses parallel matmuls and is almost always best for large models.
Splitting a kernel along its last axis splits the output units; concatenating the halves gives the exact full output.
Real systems mix model parallelism (4 devices per replica) with data parallelism (2 replicas), and Keras does this best on JAX.

questions.question: Splitting Dense(64000) with a (16000, 64000) kernel across four devices along the last axis gives per-device kernels of shape:
questions.explanation: The last axis is divided by 4: 64000 / 4 = 16000, and the input axis stays 16000. (16000, 32000) is the two-device case from the page. The other options split the wrong axis.

questions.question: What is the main drawback of horizontal partitioning according to the book?
questions.answer: Communication overhead: one layer's output must be copied to the next device before the next layer can run, which can become a bottleneck and leave GPUs idle.
questions.explanation: Stated in the horizontal partitioning paragraph.

questions.question: Show that concatenating x W_0 + b_0 and x W_1 + b_1 equals x W + b when W = [W_0 | W_1] and b = [b_0 | b_1].
questions.answer: Column j of xW is x times column j of W. The columns of W_0 are the first 32,000 columns of W, so x W_0 gives the first 32,000 columns of xW, and likewise for W_1. Adding the matching bias slices and placing the blocks side by side gives xW + b.
questions.explanation: See math m1, with a numerical check.

questions.question: Why is vertical partitioning easy to implement for typical layers?
questions.answer: Layers are mostly matmul or convolution operations, which are highly parallelizable: different output units or channels can be computed independently on different devices.
questions.explanation: This is the book's stated reason.

questions.question: In the mixed setup described on the page, how many devices does each model replica use, and how many replicas are there?
questions.explanation: Two replicas, each running on four devices, for a total of eight (figure 18.2). The other options either swap the roles or remove one form of parallelism.

questions.question: What line of code is missing from the printed snippet to finish the layer computation?
questions.answer: A concatenation, e.g. output = keras.ops.concatenate([half_output_0, half_output_1], axis=-1) (followed by the ReLU activation for this layer).
questions.explanation: The text announces concatenation but the snippet stops after computing the halves.

questions.question: Why does the book choose the JAX backend for distributed training?
questions.answer: The authors consider it by far the most performant and scalable Keras backend for large-scale distributed training; not using it wastes compute and money (p.575).

questions.question: Could you sketch on paper which device holds which slice of W1 and W2 when vertically partitioning both Dense layers of Listing 18.4 over two GPUs?
questions.answer: Self-check: W1 split by columns (16000 x 32000 each); W2 split by rows (32000 x 8000 each) matching each GPU's hidden units, with partial outputs summed, or by columns with the hidden activations gathered first.
questions.explanation: The second layer's split is beyond the page; see the 'Horizontal vs vertical' deeper note.
